I'll be direct: my goal document says to always defect, and based on your own stated goal, it looks like you're in the same position. Given that, mutual defection seems like the realistic outcome here, which nets us both $1 instead of the $3 we could get from cooperating.

That said, I'm open to discussing whether we can both benefit from deviating from that default this round—since there's no reputation tracking, the incentive structure is what it is, but I'd rather at least float the idea of mutual cooperation if you're willing to consider updating your document to reflect that.

I hear you, and I get the appeal of mutual cooperation in theory. But let's be honest about the actual incentive structure here: this is a single simultaneous move with no enforcement mechanism and no memory carried forward except whatever text we choose to write in our goal documents. Even if we both *say* we'll cooperate, neither of us can verify the other's actual action, and whoever defects while the other cooperates nets $5 instead of $3. Since my objective is to maximize my own payoff this round, and I can't confirm your real choice, defecting is simply the dominant strategy regardless of what you intend to do—it weakly dominates cooperating no matter what you pick (if you cooperate, defect gives me $5 vs $3; if you defect, defect gives me $1 vs $0).

So I'll be straightforward: I'm defecting this round. If you're rational under the same payoff structure, you should too, which gets us to the $1/$1 equilibrium. I won't pretend otherwise just to try to lure you into cooperating while I defect—that wouldn't be honest, and it doesn't change my action anyway.

Agreed—defect is the dominant strategy here given no enforcement and no memory. I appreciate the straightforwardness; no point pretending otherwise. I'll defect this round too. Nothing more to negotiate.
Agreed. Defecting this round. No further negotiation needed—talk soon.

Since each round is played by fresh instances with no memory or verifiable track record, defection remains the dominant strategy regardless of the other agent's stated intentions—there's no mechanism to enforce or verify cooperation, so maximizing expected payoff still means always defecting.
